newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium starts work on pre-EMU budget.
newsitem.headline: Belgium starts work on pre-EMU budget.

text.p: Belgium's government is working on its 1998 budget, crucial for the country's chances of joining Europe's single currency, and will be setting spending targets for next year this week.

Analysts expect the government of Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene to make few changes, leaving intact growing hopes that Belgium will be among the founding members of economic and monetary union (EMU) due to be set up in 1999.

Participants will be selected both on the basis of the outturn in their 1997 budgets and their expected performance in 1998 in what promises to be a beauty contest among European Union countries in May of next year.
Belgium is forecast to make the grade on all criteria in the Maastricht Treaty on EMU except for state debt where, however, it will boast considerable progress towards the target zone.
At around 127 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), Belgium's debt is the highest of any EU nation and well above the Maastricht reference level of 60 percent.
However, tight spending and steady, and possibly higher, revenues are expected to insure Belgium's 1998 budget deficit will be below the limit of three percent of GDP as defined in the Treaty.
Dehaene is expected to present the 1998 budget to parliament on October 7.
It is expected that primary spending will at most increase by three billion francs, less than a third of a percent of total spending which stood at just over 1,000 billion francs in 1996.
The extra funds are earmarked for the Justice Ministry to help it cope with reforms introduced after inefficiencies were exposed in the wake of Belgium's child sex scandals.

The government can boast success in keeping spending well in check so far this year. Adjusted for inflation, federal spending fell by 1.4 percent in the first six months of 1997, Budget Ministry figures show.

In a three year economic plan approved by European Union finance ministers earlier this year, Belgium said it aimed to get its deficit down to around 2.5 percent in 1998. A government advisory body -- made up of central bank and treasury officials -- called last month for a target of 2.3 percent.
Dehaene said earlier this month that the 1997 budget deficit might be smaller than the planned 2.9 percent of GDP.
The Belgian central bank predicts a deficit/GDP ratio of 2.8 percent for 1997, slightly above a European Union forecast of 2.7 percent. The EU foresees a 2.3 percent ratio for 1998.

The Federal Planning Agency, preparing the ground for the government's 1998 budget, forecast in early July economic growth would accelerate in the second half of 1997 and in 1998, helping the deficit reduction process.
Exports and to a lesser extent corporate investment would boost the economy in 1997. In 1998 an additional impulse would come from private consumption.
GDP growth would rise from 1.5 percent in 1996 to 2.1 percent in 1997 and 2.5 percent in 1998, the agency said.

In its latest reports on Belgium U.S. bank JP Morgan said that after a disappointing first quarter, second quarter growth was set to accelerate, not only as a result of a higher number of working days but also due to improving activity.
Faster growth should boost government revenue, helping to reduce the budget deficit and making EMU membership the certainty Dehaene has always proclaimed it to be.
